walkthroughs.body_html:
Ecology & the Environment — a core area of GCSE Biology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Ecology & the Environment brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Ecology & the Environment.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: The maximum sustainable population in a habitat is the:
options: Biome
Carrying capacity
Niche
Biomass

mcqs.q: Bare rock colonised by lichens is an example of:
options: Secondary succession
Primary succession
Climax community
Deflected succession

mcqs.q: Why are food chains usually limited to about 4 or 5 trophic levels?
options: Only ~10 percent of energy is transferred between trophic levels; eventually too little energy remains to support another level.
Decomposers turn dead matter into oxygen and water, with no carbon involved.
There aren't enough types of animals to fill more trophic levels.
Larger animals always eat the next ones up, and there aren't enough giant animals.

mcqs.q: How do decomposers return carbon to the atmosphere?
options: Decomposers release carbon by physically breaking matter into smaller pieces.
They respire — breaking down dead organic matter and releasing CO2.
Larger animals always eat the next ones up, and there aren't enough giant animals.
Decomposers turn dead matter into oxygen and water, with no carbon involved.

mcqs.q: Why is interspecific competition between similar species important?
options: Competition only happens between predators and their prey.
Competition means physically fighting and is rare in nature.
Decomposers turn dead matter into oxygen and water, with no carbon involved.
Two species cannot occupy exactly the same niche indefinitely — competition often leads to displacement or niche divergence.
